newsitem.title: USA: U.S. analysts see rift as Ecuador FinMin wants out.
newsitem.headline: U.S. analysts see rift as Ecuador FinMin wants out.

text.p: The tendered resignation of Ecuador's Finance Minister shows a deepening rift between politicians and technocrats over economic policies, U.S. analysts said.
Ecuador Finance Minister Carlos Davalos confirmed on Thursday that he had submitted his resignation, after days of rumors that he would quit.
The reluctance of President Fabian Alarcon's government to reduce the fiscal deficit put the "technical side" in a difficult situation, said Pablo Goldberg, senior economist at Smith Barney.
By "technical side," he referred to the economic team of Davalos, which includes central bank chief Fidel Jaramillo and head of the monetary board Danilo Carrera.
Without tough fiscal measures, Ecuador is unable to satisfy the Paris Club creditors, which in turn precludes it from getting a standby loan from the International Monetary Fund, Goldberg said.
"Ecuador is in a vicious cycle," he said.
The market was abuzz with rumors that Jaramillo and Carrera were also about to quit. An aide to Jaramillo said the central bank chief had not tendered his resignation.
The economic team's frustration mounted over Alarcon's proposal to reduce the fiscal deficit, which amounted to monetizing the external debt, said Siobhan Manning, analyst at Santader Securities.
"The resignation could mean more frictions in the cabinet," she said.
But Davalos's decision to leave could have also been prompted by personal reasons because he was in frail health, Manning said.
More important to watch was whether Jaramillo and Carrera would also throw in the towel, she said.
Of the trio, Jaramillo is the central figure because he has cultivated good ties with the U.S. investment community over the years, she said. "Jaramillo's resignation would be catastrophic."
In a visit to New York early this month, Jaramillo assured the U.S. investment community that the economic team would stay intact after Alarcon appointed his cabinet.
Ecuador PDI ECPDI=RR plunged 1-3/8 to 64-3/4 bid on Davalos's resignation news.

If the selloff sent President Alarcon a message on how foreign investors' confidence was shaken by the change of the economic team, he might make compromises to keep Jaramillo on the job, Manning said.
Carlos Janada, analyst at Morgan Stanley, said the market had limited hope that Alarcon would take any tough fiscal measures before he could win a full term in next year's election.
Davalos's departure, seen in this context, would probably change very little, he said. "We remain neutral on Ecuador."

Javier Murcio, senior Latin America economist at CS First Boston, said the referendum in May gave Alarcon a clear mandate until the next election, which he could use to his advantage to implement some changes.
Before it becomes clear why Davalos resigned, it is premature to speculate what path his successor might take to steer the economy, he said.
